README: Source list for translators. Make <code>.json with meta {name (the language in itself), title, page_title, tag, desc (~200 chars), meta_desc (~150 chars), doc_title (<title>), og_locale (hi_IN), locale (Intl, e.g. hi-IN), dir (ltr|rtl), lang_label (the word Language)} and s {English key: translation} for every key in strings. Keep {placeholders}, HTML tags and their attributes exactly, &entities;, emoji, numbers, units (dB, LUFS, dBTP, Hz, kbps, MB), keyboard keys (Space, Ctrl+Z, B, N, Esc ...) and names (MES Audio Editor, DeepFilterNet, RNNoise, Audacity, Camtasia, YouTube, Spotify, MP3, WAV, M4A, AAC ...). Never use the ASCII double quote character inside a translation (use typographic quotes): many strings go into HTML attributes. Natural, everyday wording, not word for word. Check: node tool_apps_src/audio/i18n/extract.js --check

How far the noise is pushed down. 100% removes as much as the AI can (often 40 dB or more: the noise is gone). 50% turns it down by about 20 dB (a quarter of its loudness is a lot of difference, but some room sound stays, which can sound more natural). 0% changes nothing. Move it while the preview plays to hear the difference.

Mains hum is a low, steady buzz at the frequency of the electricity in the walls: 60 Hz in North America and parts of South America, 50 Hz in Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia. It comes from power cables near the microphone, cheap power adapters, lights, or a ground loop (two devices plugged into different sockets). It sounds like a deep "hmmm" that is there even when nobody talks.
Remove (detect) finds which one it is and notches exactly that frequency and its overtones, leaving the voice alone. Choose Leave if you hear no buzz.

Which tool cleans the sound.
DeepFilterNet 3 is an AI trained on thousands of hours of speech: it keeps the voice and removes almost everything else (fans, air conditioning, traffic, hiss, keyboard, room noise). Best choice for talking, podcasts and videos.
RNNoise is a smaller AI: faster, a little gentler.
Spectral gate is the classic method: it learns what the noise sounds like from a few seconds with no voice, then turns that sound down. Use it for music or for one steady sound (hiss, a hum, a fridge).
A low, steady buzz from the electricity: 60 Hz in North America, 50 Hz in Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia. Detect finds which one your recording has.
